source.title: Beyond I'm Sorry, I Can't: Dissecting Large Language Model Refusal
source.authors: Nirmalendu Prakash; Wei Jie Yeo; Amirali Abdullah; Ranjan Satapathy; Erik Cambria; Roy Ka-Wei Lee

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equations and table layouts are flattened or affected by line breaks, but the results relevant here are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies SAE feature identification and ablation to refusal in two instruction-tuned LLMs, reporting whether recovered features affect refusal. It does not test superposition geometry in toy networks.
record.gate_note: Rows below record the study's own SAE-feature ablation results and controls. Prior-work results and diagnostic values used to choose directions, layers, or hyperparameters are not recorded as findings. The paper does not measure feature overlap geometry or compare feature count with representation dimension.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained Gemmascope and Llamascope SAEs as a tool to find refusal-relevant latents. It reports how well its own three-stage pipeline jailbreaks models when those latents are ablated, compared against random features, a linear probe and an O'Brien et al. baseline. It never asks whether features are superposed, spread across neurons, sparse beyond SAE design, or recovered faithfully by the SAE. Nor does it test completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features, or their dimensionality. Ablation success rates measure the pipeline's selection quality, not any version of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that their SAE-plus-factorization-machine pipeline isolates causal refusal features, and that FMs beat linear probes, showing non-linear interactions. They also report dormant redundant 'hydra' features and give a taxonomy mapping. The interaction direction differs by model: Stage 3→Stage 2 dependency is strong in LLaMA and diffuse in Gemma. Yet Gemma shows 100% Stage 2→Stage 3 deactivation, so 'stronger interaction in LLaMA' is an oversimplification.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE feature selection, ablation, and factorization machines on LLM refusal; it does not reproduce toy-network superposition experiments or their geometry measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary between Gemma and LLaMA and between Stage 2, Stage 3, and Stage 3-only feature sets. LLaMA's Stage 3-only set is reported effective, whereas Gemma's is not. The paper also states that different FM embedding sizes affect feature representation and that its K sweep is limited by degenerate outputs or computational constraints.

fits_no_version.finding: Some SAE latents flagged as refusal-critical are inactive on the prompt (77 in LLaMA, 1656 in Gemma), yet needed for jailbreak. Ablating active latents makes them switch on, which the authors read as a hydra-like redundancy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents in LLMs interact non-additively: suppressing some latents activates dormant ones that compensate for them.

fits_no_version.finding: Harm-category labels for features derived from their activations matched human labels from Neuronpedia explanations and top activations with only 13.42% accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-based and explanation-based interpretations of SAE features often disagree.

record.problems: The study tests only two model sizes. Its authors note SAE sensitivity to data and initialization and cite approximately 30% latent overlap across seeds, but do not replicate across SAE runs. Some comparisons lack a clearly stated baseline in the reported passage, and SAE feature explanations received only 13.42% accuracy against activation-based labels in the human study.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. The paper's cross-entropy comparisons assess downstream language-model loss rather than whether SAE features are recovered as representational units. Feature steering on benign prompts is intentionally induced and does not establish naturally occurring superposition.

untested.parts: All of it: toy networks, overlap geometry, sparsity transition.
All of it: capacity competition and dedicated dimensions.
All of it: non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Whether features spread across many neurons and whether SAEs recover genuine sparse features. SAEs are assumed, not tested.
Completeness, stability across seeds and canonicity. The authors cite ~30% seed overlap but do not test it.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' and its V4 labels are overturned: the paper treats SAE latents as given units and evaluates a jailbreak-feature search. The Table 1/2 'ASR (no ablation)' entries (4, 71) are on an unclear scale relative to the after-ablation fractions. The r2 'absent' state is therefore unsupported.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network feature storage, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The study tests whether SAE latents can be identified and causally intervened on in two LLMs. It does not measure how features are distributed across neurons, quantify sparsity or superposition, or test other model families.
The study does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable across runs, or canonical units.
The study uses individual SAE decoder vectors but does not compare one-dimensional with multidimensional feature representations.

relation.reason: Uses SAE decomposition as a tool; does not independently test superposition, dictionary completeness or stability, capacity pressure, or feature dimensionality.

tranche.reason: Uses pretrained SAEs to develop and evaluate a refusal-feature discovery pipeline. Its reported outcomes measure jailbreak performance and feature interactions, without testing a superposition claim version.

source_check.notes: All eleven rows describe pipeline performance or internal controls and appropriately link to no claim version. Preserve baseline entries 4 and 71 as printed; neither their normalization nor a quantitative ablation comparison can be established from those entries.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Ablating the recovered Stage 3 SAE features was reported sufficient for 330/372 cases; random-feature ablation produced no jailbreaks (r6, r10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Effects varied by model and feature set: Gemma Stage 3-only ablation yielded 8 cases, while LLaMA Stage 2 ASR was nearly unchanged from the no-ablation entry (r1–r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Removing inactive selected features reduced reported success, while random ablation yielded no LLaMA jailbreaks and only 5 Gemma samples; the paper therefore reports dependencies and model-specific results rather than a uniform feature effect (r7–r10).
